title: "Undoing Mistakes"

# Undoing Mistakes

After this page you can discard an unstaged edit, unstage a file, and rewrite the last commit **before anyone else has it**.

## Three common “undo”s

| You did | You want | Command |
|---------|----------|---------|
| Edited a tracked file, not staged | Throw the edit away | `git restore <file>` |
| `git add` too soon | Keep the edit, leave it out of the next commit | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Last commit message (or last commit contents) is wrong, not pushed | Replace that commit | `git commit --amend` |

These are safe on a laptop branch nobody has fetched. After `git push`, amending rewrites a hash other people may have. Chapter 9 and chapter 11 cover that case. Chapter 17 (reflog) is the safety net when you went too far.

```text
 restore <file>              restore --staged           commit --amend
 working ← index             index ← HEAD               A ← B ← C
                                                        A ← B ← C'   (C gone from main)
```

## Discard unstaged work

```bash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "oops" >> README.md
git restore README.md
```

The working-tree file matches the index again. The “oops” line is gone. Git cannot get it back from Git; your editor’s undo might.

Restore one file from HEAD even if it was staged:

```bash
git restore --source=HEAD --worktree --staged README.md
```

That is “make this file look like the last commit, in both index and working tree.”

## Unstage, keep the edit

```bash
echo "keep me" >> README.md
git add README.md
git restore --staged README.md
git status
```

The line is still in the file. It is not in the index. The next `git commit` will not include it until you `git add` again.

Older docs say `git reset HEAD README.md` for the same unstage. This book uses `git restore --staged`.

## Amend the last commit

You just committed and noticed a typo in the message:

```bash
git commit --amend -m "Add ping helper"
```

You forgot a file:

```bash
git add src/ping.py
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

`--no-edit` keeps the old message. `--amend` replaces the last commit with a new one (new hash) whose parent is the same as before. `git log` no longer shows the old hash as `main`. The old commit is still in the reflog for about 30 days (chapter 17).

Amend only when:

- it is the latest commit on this branch, and
- you have not pushed it, or you are sure no one else built on it.

## Revert is a new commit

`git revert <hash>` adds a commit that undoes a previous one. Use it on history other people already have. Chapter 10 is revert and cherry-pick. For a local last-commit mistake, amend. For an old published mistake, revert.

## `rm` and `mv`

```bash
git rm src/old.py              # stop tracking and delete the file
git rm --cached secrets.env    # stop tracking, keep the file on disk
git mv src/ping.py src/health.py
git status
git commit -m "Rename ping to health"
```

`git mv` is `mv` plus `git add` of the rename. Git detects renames in diffs even if you `mv` and `add` by hand; `git mv` is the tidy form.

## If you are lost

```bash
git status
git log --oneline -5
```

Status tells you which of the three trees disagree. Log tells you where `main` points. The hands-on page next builds a tiny `desk-api` from scratch so you can practice the whole loop, including one amend.
